OPEN
This is open, and cannot be resolved with a finite computation.
Let $R(k,l)$ be the usual Ramsey number: the smallest $n$ such that if the edges of $K_n$ are coloured red and blue then there exists either a red $K_k$ or a blue $K_l$.
Prove the existence of some $c>0$ such that\[\lim_{k\to \infty}\frac{R(k+1,k)}{R(k,k)}> 1+c.\]
#1030: [Er93,p.339]
graph theory | 
ramsey theory
A problem of Erdős and Sós, who could not even prove whether $R(k+1,k)-R(k,k)>k^c$ for any $c>1$.
It is trivial that $R(k+1,k)-R(k,k)\geq k-2$. Burr, Erdős, Faudree, and Schelp [BEFS89] proved\[R(k+1,k)-R(k,k)\geq 2k-5.\]See also [544] for a similar question concerning $R(3,k)$, and [1014] for the general off-diagonal case.
Additional thanks to: Ryan Tuck

 The way this problem is phrased could probably be improved ("the Ramsey number"?) and it appears the limit needs defining (is that k -> infinity?). I don't have access to the source but am working on contributing a formalization at https://github.com/google-deepmind/formal-conjectures/pull/3588 and this was raised as an issue :)

 Yes, I meant that $R(k,l)$ is the off-diagonal Ramsey number defined in the usual way, and the limit should be interpreted as $k\to\infty$ (this is a common convention on this site where I just write $\lim$ if the variable in question and the endpoint is obvious from context; albeit confusing in this instance because I did write the variable but not the endpoint, I'm not sure why).
